```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r libs}
library(anovakit)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
# Formatting helpers for numbers quoted in the prose.
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
fp <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", f3(p))
```

`anova_glm()` fits a generalised linear model of a response on one or more
grouping factors, in any `family`, and reports an analysis of deviance table,
effect sizes, marginal means and pairwise comparisons. With the default
Gaussian family it is an ordinary factorial analysis of variance. Other
families model responses whose spread changes with their mean.

Four functions cover particular cases better. For a one-way comparison of
means with unequal variances, `anova_welch()` is better calibrated
([walkthrough](welch.html)). For 0/1 outcomes use `anova_bin()`
([walkthrough](binary.html)), and for counts `anova_count()`
([walkthrough](counts.html)): both add diagnostics and effect sizes that
`anova_glm()` does not. To adjust for a numeric covariate use
`anova_ancova()` ([walkthrough](ancova.html)).

This walkthrough follows two analyses side by side: a Gaussian two-way ANOVA,
and a Gamma model for prices.

## The data

`ToothGrowth` records the length of odontoblasts (the cells responsible for
tooth growth) in 60 guinea pigs. Each animal received vitamin C at one of
three doses (0.5, 1 or 2 mg/day) by one of two delivery methods: orange juice
(`OJ`) or ascorbic acid (`VC`). `dose` is stored as a number; here it is a
grouping variable with three levels, so make it a factor.

```{r data}
tg <- ToothGrowth
tg$dose <- factor(tg$dose)
table(tg$supp, tg$dose)
round(tapply(tg$len, list(tg$supp, tg$dose), mean), 2)
```

This is a balanced 2 x 3 design with ten animals per cell. Besides whether
dose and supplement matter, the question is whether the effect of the
supplement depends on the dose. The cell means suggest it does: orange juice
is ahead at the two lower doses, but not at 2 mg/day.

`MASS::Cars93` lists 93 car models on sale in the US in 1993. Their `Price`
(in thousands of dollars) is positive and right-skewed, and within each
`Type` of car the spread grows with the typical price:

```{r cars}
cars <- MASS::Cars93[, c("Manufacturer", "Model", "Type", "Price")]
price <- split(cars$Price, cars$Type)
cs <- t(sapply(price, function(x) c(n = length(x), median = median(x),
                                    mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x),
                                    cv = sd(x) / mean(x))))
round(cs, 2)
```

A Gaussian model assumes the same standard deviation in every group, and here
it ranges from `r f2(cs["Van", "sd"])` for vans to `r f2(cs["Midsize", "sd"])`
for midsize cars. A Gamma
family assumes instead that the standard deviation is proportional to the
mean, a constant coefficient of variation (`cv`). The `cv` column fits that
better, though not perfectly: vans are unusually uniform.

## Fitting the model

Columns are named as character strings. With `interaction = TRUE` the model
contains both factors and their interaction. Listing `dose` first puts it on
the x axis of the marginal-means plot.

```{r fit}
fit <- anova_glm(tg, "len", c("dose", "supp"), interaction = TRUE)
fit
```

The first line names the family, the link and the type of sums of squares; a
Gaussian family with the identity link is an ordinary linear model.
`Observations used: 60` says no rows were dropped. The heading
`Omnibus test (Type II, F)` names the type of test and the statistic, which
the table itself does not show. There is no `Notes` block because nothing
needed saying, and `Plots available` lists the four plots in `$plots`.
`summary(fit)` adds the assumption checks, the effect sizes, the marginal
means and the pairwise comparisons.

For the car prices, a Gamma family with a log link makes the group effects
multiplicative, so comparisons come out as ratios of means:

```{r gamma-fit}
gam <- anova_glm(cars, "Price", "Type", family = Gamma(link = "log"))
gam
```

`family` accepts a family object, as here, a family function, or a name such
as `"Gamma"`. The name alone gives the Gamma family's default inverse link,
which is rarely what you want for group comparisons (see
[below](#the-link-decides-what-a-comparison-is)). The note explains why one
effect size is `NA`; [Effect sizes](#effect-sizes) has the details.

## The omnibus test

```{r anova}
fit$anova
```

`term` names the effect, and `dose:supp` is the interaction. `sum_sq` and
`df` are each term's sum of squares and degrees of freedom; the `Residuals`
row holds the error sum of squares. `statistic` is the F statistic, the
term's mean square over the residual mean square, and `p_value` its p-value.

The interaction is significant (F = `r f2(fit$anova$statistic[3])`,
p `r fp(fit$anova$p_value[3])`): the supplement effect is not the same at
every dose. A main-effect row averages over a pattern that changes, so read
the cell means and comparisons below rather than the main effects alone.

### Type II or Type III

With `type = "II"` (the default) each main effect is tested after the other
main effect, but not after the interaction. With `type = "III"` every term is
tested after every other, interaction included. In a balanced design like
this one the two coincide:

```{r type-balanced}
fit3 <- anova_glm(tg, "len", c("dose", "supp"), interaction = TRUE,
                  type = "III", plots = FALSE)
fit3$anova
```

They differ when the cells are unequal. Suppose four animals had been lost
from the `VC`, 2 mg cell and two from the `OJ`, 0.5 mg cell:

```{r type-unbalanced}
lost <- c(which(tg$supp == "VC" & tg$dose == "2")[1:4],
          which(tg$supp == "OJ" & tg$dose == "0.5")[1:2])
tg_u <- tg[-lost, ]
table(tg_u$supp, tg_u$dose)
anova_glm(tg_u, "len", c("dose", "supp"), interaction = TRUE,
          plots = FALSE)$anova
anova_glm(tg_u, "len", c("dose", "supp"), interaction = TRUE,
          type = "III", plots = FALSE)$anova
```

The interaction row is the same in both, because it is adjusted for
everything either way; the main-effect rows differ. Type II has more
power to detect a main effect when there is no interaction. Type III tests
each main effect averaged over the levels of the other factor, weighting each
cell equally, which some analysts prefer when an interaction is present
because it does not depend on the cell sizes.

### Type III is fitted under sum-to-zero contrasts

A Type III test of `supp` removes the columns that code `supp` while keeping
the interaction, and what that tests depends on how the factors are coded.
Under R's default treatment contrasts, the `supp` columns describe the
supplement effect at the reference dose only, so the "Type III" row for
`supp` tests the supplement at 0.5 mg/day. Under sum-to-zero contrasts it
tests the supplement effect averaged over the doses, which is what a main
effect means. So with `type = "III"`, `anova_glm()` fits the model under
`contr.sum`. Setting `options(contrasts = )` after fitting would not help,
because the contrasts are stored on the fitted model. Here is what fitting
with the defaults and asking `car::Anova()` for Type III gives:

```{r naive-type3}
naive <- glm(len ~ dose * supp, data = tg)    # treatment contrasts
naive_tab <- car::Anova(naive, type = 3, test.statistic = "F")
naive_tab
unlist(fit3$model$contrasts)
```

The `supp` row has F = `r f2(naive_tab["supp", "F values"])`, the test of the
supplement at the reference dose, not the
F = `r f2(fit3$anova$statistic[2])` of the averaged main effect. The contrasts stored on `fit3$model` (`contr.sum`) are what make its
Type III row a test of the averaged effect.

### Choosing the test statistic

`test_statistic = NULL` (the default) chooses the test after fitting. A
family that estimates its dispersion, like the Gaussian and the Gamma, gets
an F test, and a family whose dispersion is fixed at 1 (binomial, Poisson)
gets a likelihood-ratio test. In the F table of a non-Gaussian family the
`sum_sq` column holds deviances: the `Type` row is the drop in deviance when
`Type` is added, and the `Residuals` row is the Pearson chi-squared
statistic, which divided by its degrees of freedom gives the dispersion. F is
the ratio of the two per degree of freedom:

```{r f-by-hand}
a <- gam$anova
a
(a$sum_sq[1] / a$df[1]) / (a$sum_sq[2] / a$df[2])
```

`"LR"` and `"Wald"` give the other two statistics. The columns come in the
same order whatever the statistic, and only an F table has `sum_sq` and a
`Residuals` row:

```{r test-statistic}
for (ts in c("LR", "Wald")) {
  g <- anova_glm(cars, "Price", "Type", family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                 test_statistic = ts, plots = FALSE)
  cat("\n", attr(g$anova, "statistic"), "\n", sep = "")
  print(g$anova)
}
```

All three agree that the car types differ. For a family that estimates its
dispersion, the "LR" statistic is not a true likelihood ratio. It is the
deviance drop divided by the estimated dispersion, referred to a chi-squared
distribution as though the dispersion were known, and the heading calls it a
scaled-deviance chi-square. It ignores the uncertainty in the dispersion,
which the F test allows for, so F is the better default there. A quasi
family has no likelihood, so `test_statistic = "LR"` gives the F test, with a
note. The Wald test is built from the coefficients and their covariance, and
is the only one of the three that can use robust standard errors (see
[Options](#options)).

## Effect sizes

For a Gaussian model `$effect_sizes` holds partial eta squared and partial
omega squared for each term, from the sums of squares of the F table:

```{r effect-sizes}
fit$effect_sizes
```

`partial_eta_sq` is the term's sum of squares over itself plus the residual
sum of squares: the share of the variance not explained by the other terms
that this term explains. Dose accounts for
`r round(100 * fit$effect_sizes$partial_eta_sq[1])`% of it.
`partial_omega_sq` corrects eta squared for its upward bias in samples, so it
is a little smaller; a negative value is floored at 0, with a note. Both are
partial, so they do not add up to 1 across terms and are not a partition of
the total variance.

Any other family has no sums of squares, so the effect size is
`deviance_explained`, 1 minus the residual deviance over the null deviance:

```{r gamma-effects}
gam$effect_sizes
```

Car type explains `r round(100 * gam$effect_sizes$estimate[1])`% of the
deviance. McFadden's pseudo R squared (`mcfadden_r2`) is reported only for
the binomial, Poisson and negative binomial families. For a Gamma model it is
`NA`, because the log-likelihood of a density shifts with the units of the
response, and the note says so.

## Marginal means and comparisons

Because the ToothGrowth model contains the interaction, the marginal means
are for the six cells. For a Gaussian model with the identity link they are
the cell means, with intervals that use the pooled residual variance:

```{r emmeans}
fit$emmeans
```

`$posthoc` compares every pair of cells, 15 in all, with a Tukey adjustment
by default. The three comparisons of the supplements at the same dose are:

```{r posthoc}
same_dose <- c("dose0.5 OJ - dose0.5 VC", "dose1 OJ - dose1 VC",
               "dose2 OJ - dose2 VC")
ph <- fit$posthoc
print(ph[ph$contrast %in% same_dose, ], digits = 3)
```

`estimate` is the first cell minus the second. `conf_low` and `conf_high` are
Tukey-adjusted (simultaneous) intervals. `p_value` is unadjusted, and
`p_adjusted` is adjusted across all 15 comparisons. Orange juice gives longer
odontoblasts than ascorbic acid at 0.5 and 1 mg/day, and the two are
indistinguishable at 2 mg/day.

If only those three comparisons interest you, adjusting for all 15 is more
conservative than it needs to be. `$emmeans_object` is the emmeans grid,
so you can ask for exactly the family of comparisons you want. It carries
emmeans' own default level, so give `level =` explicitly:

```{r emm-object}
by_dose <- emmeans::contrast(fit$emmeans_object, method = "pairwise",
                             by = "dose")
summary(by_dose, infer = TRUE, level = fit$conf_level)
```

With one comparison per dose there is nothing to adjust within each family.
[Working with results](results.html) covers `$emmeans_object` further.

### Ratios on the log scale

The Gamma model's marginal means are on the response scale, in thousands of
dollars. In a one-factor model they are the group means. Their intervals are
computed on the log scale and back-transformed, so they are not symmetric
about the estimate:

```{r gamma-emmeans}
gam$emmeans
```

With a log link a pairwise comparison is a ratio of means, in a column called
`ratio`, tested against 1. These are the comparisons that survive Tukey's
adjustment:

```{r gamma-posthoc}
gph <- gam$posthoc
print(gph[gph$p_adjusted < 0.05,
          c("contrast", "ratio", "conf_low", "conf_high", "p_adjusted")],
      digits = 3)
```

Midsize cars, for example, average
`r f2(gph$ratio[gph$contrast == "Midsize / Small"])` times the price of small
ones.

### The link decides what a comparison is

With the log link comparisons are ratios, and with the logit link they are
odds ratios. With any other non-identity link they are differences between
the means on the response scale, and `$notes` says so. The Gamma family's
default link is the inverse:

```{r inverse-link}
inv <- anova_glm(cars, "Price", "Type", family = "Gamma", plots = FALSE)
inv$method
inv$notes[grepl("link", inv$notes)]
head(inv$posthoc[, c("contrast", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_high")], 3)
```

### The coefficient table

The fitted coefficients are in `$assumptions$coefficients`:

```{r coefficients}
fit$assumptions$coefficients
```

The table has t statistics (the dispersion is estimated) and
profile-likelihood intervals by default, which for a Gaussian model equal
`confint(lm())`. Under the default treatment contrasts the intercept is the
mean of the reference cell (0.5 mg/day, orange juice), and the other
coefficients are differences from it. `fit3`, fitted under sum-to-zero
contrasts, has different coefficients for the same fitted values: the
intercept is the average of the six cell means, `dose1` is the average for
0.5 mg/day minus that grand mean, and `supp1` the average for orange juice
minus it.

```{r coefficients-sum}
fit3$assumptions$coefficients[, c("term", "estimate")]
mean(fit$emmeans$estimate)
```

The Gamma coefficients are on the log scale:

```{r gamma-coefficients}
co <- gam$assumptions$coefficients
co
```

The intercept is the log of the mean price of the reference type, `Compact`,
and each other coefficient is the log of a ratio to it: small cars cost
exp(`r f3(co$estimate[4])`) = `r f2(exp(co$estimate[4]))` times as much as
compact ones on average. The `distribution` column says the tests use t,
because the dispersion is estimated.

## Checking assumptions

A Gaussian model assumes independent observations, normally distributed
errors and the same error variance in every cell. `$assumptions` holds the
dispersion, and the plots in the next section cover normality.

### Dispersion

```{r dispersion}
fit$assumptions$dispersion
sqrt(fit$assumptions$dispersion)
```

`dispersion` is the Pearson dispersion: the sum of squared Pearson residuals
divided by the residual degrees of freedom. For a Gaussian model that is the
residual mean square, so its square root,
`r f2(sqrt(fit$assumptions$dispersion))`, is the residual standard deviation
in the units of the response. There is no formal test of equal variances;
compare the cell standard deviations:

```{r cell-sds}
cell_sd <- tapply(tg$len, list(tg$supp, tg$dose), sd)
round(cell_sd, 2)
```

They range from `r f2(min(cell_sd))` to `r f2(max(cell_sd))`, so the largest
cell variance is `r f2((max(cell_sd) / min(cell_sd))^2)` times the smallest.
With ten animals in every cell, a balanced design tolerates that well. If the
variances differed badly, use robust standard errors (`vcov_type`, under
[Options](#options)) or, for a one-way design, `anova_welch()`.

For a Gamma family the dispersion is the squared coefficient of variation:

```{r gamma-dispersion}
gam$assumptions$dispersion
sqrt(gam$assumptions$dispersion)
```

The model puts the standard deviation of prices at about
`r round(100 * sqrt(gam$assumptions$dispersion))`% of the mean in every car
type. The observed values in [the data](#the-data) range from
`r round(100 * cs["Van", "cv"])`% (vans) to
`r round(100 * cs["Midsize", "cv"])`% (midsize cars), so the constant-CV
assumption is only roughly true; the `vcov_type` option below protects the
comparisons against that.

### Is Gamma the right family?

The vans show that the Gamma variance function is not exact. To check that it
still describes the prices better than the Gaussian, compare the two fits by
AIC. `$model_stats` holds the AIC, BIC, null and residual deviances and
residual degrees of freedom, and `$family` is the family object used. The Gaussian and
Gamma fits are full likelihoods for the same response, so their AICs can be
compared directly:

```{r aic}
str(gam$model_stats)
gau <- anova_glm(cars, "Price", "Type", plots = FALSE)
c(gaussian = gau$model_stats$AIC, gamma = gam$model_stats$AIC)
```

The Gamma model has the lower AIC by
`r round(gau$model_stats$AIC - gam$model_stats$AIC)`. The
[diagnostics guide](diagnostics.html) covers the checks across the package.

## Plots

`fit` has four plots. The `box` plot is the raw data behind the means: the
observed lengths in each cell, ordered by median and labelled with the cell
size.

```{r plot-box}
plot(fit, "box")
```

In the `emmeans` plot the gap between the supplements closes at 2 mg/day.
Dose, the first grouping factor, is on the x axis, and the supplement sets the
colour, with one line per supplement, so lines that are not parallel are the
interaction. The error bars are intervals for each mean at `conf_level`.

```{r plot-emmeans}
plot(fit, "emmeans")
```

```{r emm-2mg, include = FALSE}
at2 <- fit$emmeans$estimate[fit$emmeans$dose == "2"]
```

The `residuals` and `qq` plots check the Gaussian assumptions:

```{r plot-resid-qq, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%", fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
plot(fit, "residuals")
plot(fit, "qq")
```

On the left, the deviance residuals (for a Gaussian model, the ordinary
residuals) are plotted against the fitted values. They fall in vertical
stripes, one per cell mean. The two 2 mg/day cells have almost the same mean
(`r f2(at2[1])` and `r f2(at2[2])`), so their stripes overlap. Stripes of
clearly different heights mean unequal variances, and a funnel that widens
with the fitted value means a variance that grows with the mean, which
suggests another family. Here the heights vary somewhat, as the cell standard
deviations did, but there is no funnel.

On the right, the Q-Q plot compares the residuals with a normal distribution;
systematic curvature at the ends would mean skewness or heavy tails. The
points follow the line well. The lower tail is a little shorter than a normal
one, a mild departure for a balanced design with 60 observations.

If the variance of a Gamma model really is proportional to the mean squared,
its deviance residuals have roughly the same spread at every fitted value.
For the car prices the stripes differ in height:

```{r gamma-residuals}
plot(gam, "residuals")
```

In a one-factor model the fitted values are the group means. Two stripes sit
side by side: vans (`r f2(cs["Van", "mean"])`) on the left and sporty cars
(`r f2(cs["Sporty", "mean"])`) on the right. The vans' stripe is by far the
shortest, because their prices vary much less than the model assumes. The
midsize stripe, at `r f2(cs["Midsize", "mean"])`, is the tallest.

The deviance residuals of a Gamma model are approximately normal when the
model fits. Here the middle follows the line and the upper tail rises above
it, so a few cars are dearer than a Gamma distribution with this dispersion
would predict.

```{r gamma-qq}
plot(gam, "qq")
```

`gam$model` is an ordinary `glm`, so you can find those cars directly:

```{r gamma-top}
res <- residuals(gam$model, type = "deviance")
head(cars[order(res, decreasing = TRUE), ], 3)
```

The Gamma `emmeans` plot shows the means on the response scale, with their
asymmetric intervals. `Type` has no natural order, so the points are not
joined by a line; lines appear only across a second grouping factor, as in
the ToothGrowth plot. The fourth plot, `plot(gam, "box")`, shows the raw
prices by type.

```{r gamma-emm-plot}
plot(gam, "emmeans")
```

All plots are ggplot2 objects that you can change with `+`; see
[Plots and themes](visuals.html).

## Options

### `ci_method`

`ci_method = "profile"` (the default) cuts the profile likelihood at the t
quantiles the tests beside it use. The p-values are Wald p-values, though, so
in a small sample a profile interval can exclude 0 while its p-value is above
0.05, or the reverse; `$notes` names any such row. `ci_method = "wald"` gives
estimate ± t × SE, which always agrees with the p-value:

```{r ci-method}
wald <- anova_glm(cars, "Price", "Type", family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                  ci_method = "wald", plots = FALSE)$assumptions$coefficients
cbind(co[, c("term", "estimate")],
      profile = co[, c("conf_low", "conf_high")],
      wald = wald[, c("conf_low", "conf_high")])
```

The two differ in the third decimal place here. Profile intervals follow the
shape of the likelihood, which matters more in small samples or near a
boundary; Wald intervals are symmetric on the log scale. Exponentiate either
to get an interval for the ratio.

### `vcov_type`

`vcov_type` takes an HC type (`"HC0"` to `"HC4"`) from the sandwich
package. The robust covariance does not rely on the family's variance
function, so it protects the marginal means and comparisons when that
function is wrong, as the vans suggest it is here:

```{r vcov}
rob <- anova_glm(cars, "Price", "Type", family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                 vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)
cbind(rob$emmeans[, "Type", drop = FALSE],
      se_model = gam$emmeans$se, se_HC3 = rob$emmeans$se)
grep("omnibus|Robust", rob$notes, value = TRUE)
```

The standard error for vans shrinks and the one for midsize cars grows: each
now reflects that type's own spread. The robust covariance reaches the
coefficient table (with Wald intervals, since a profile likelihood cannot use
it), the marginal means and the comparisons. The omnibus F test compares
deviances and does not use it; `test_statistic = "Wald"` gives an omnibus
test that does:

```{r vcov-wald}
anova_glm(cars, "Price", "Type", family = Gamma(link = "log"),
          vcov_type = "HC3", test_statistic = "Wald", plots = FALSE)$anova
```

[Weights and robust standard errors](weights.html) covers `vcov_type` across
the package, including when the function falls back to the model-based
covariance.

### `weights`

`weights` names a column of prior weights, and what a weight means depends
on the family and the response. Whole numbers on a 0/1 response or on counts
(binomial, Poisson and negative binomial families) are frequency weights,
and whole numbers on a binomial proportion are numbers of trials. Any other
weights, including all weights in the Gaussian and Gamma families, are used
as `glm()` uses them, with each row one unit.
[Weights and robust standard errors](weights.html) sets out the rules; this
section shows one use.

A response that is itself an average suits a Gamma model with weights. The
mean of m prices has variance φμ²/m, so its prior weight is m. Suppose you
had only the average price per manufacturer and type, with the number of
models behind each:

```{r weights-data}
agg <- aggregate(Price ~ Manufacturer + Type, data = cars, FUN = mean)
agg$n_models <- aggregate(Price ~ Manufacturer + Type, data = cars,
                          FUN = length)$Price
table(agg$n_models)
```

Weighting each average by its count recovers the marginal means of the full
data exactly; ignoring the counts does not:

```{r weights-fit}
w_fit <- anova_glm(agg, "Price", "Type", family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                   weights = "n_models", plots = FALSE)
u_fit <- anova_glm(agg, "Price", "Type", family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                   plots = FALSE)
data.frame(Type = gam$emmeans$Type, full_data = gam$emmeans$estimate,
           weighted = w_fit$emmeans$estimate,
           unweighted = u_fit$emmeans$estimate)
```

The standard errors differ slightly from the full-data fit, because the
dispersion is now estimated from `r nrow(agg)` averages rather than
`r nrow(cars)` cars. A row with weight zero is dropped before fitting,
counted in `$n_removed` and recorded in `$notes`.

### `interaction`

The default, `interaction = FALSE`, fits the grouping factors additively. The
marginal means and comparisons are then reported for each factor on its own,
averaged over the others, with a `term` column saying which, and each
factor's comparisons form their own multiplicity family:

```{r additive}
add <- anova_glm(tg, "len", c("dose", "supp"), plots = FALSE)
add$emmeans
add$notes
```

`interaction = TRUE` fits the full factorial. With three or more factors a
whole number sets the highest order of interaction: `interaction = 2` keeps
the two-way interactions and drops the rest.

### `adjust`, `conf_level` and `posthoc`

`adjust` is applied by emmeans and accepts `"tukey"` (the default),
`"sidak"`, `"scheffe"`, `"dunnettx"`, `"bonferroni"`, `"holm"`,
`"hochberg"`, `"hommel"`, `"BH"`, `"BY"`, `"fdr"` or `"none"`. A step-down
method such as Holm cannot be turned into intervals, so emmeans gives
Bonferroni intervals beside Holm p-values, and `$notes` says so:

```{r adjust}
holm <- anova_glm(tg, "len", c("dose", "supp"), interaction = TRUE,
                  adjust = "holm", plots = FALSE)
holm$notes
```

`conf_level` sets the level of every interval: the coefficient table, the
marginal means and the comparisons. `posthoc = FALSE` skips the pairwise
comparisons, of which there are `choose(k, 2)` for k cells (counted per factor
in an additive model); `$notes` records that they were skipped and how many
there would have been.

## What the notes say

```{r notes}
fit$notes
gam$notes
```

The ToothGrowth fit has no notes: no rows were dropped, the model is far from
saturated, nothing failed to compute, and the Gaussian family has partial eta
squared to report. The Gamma fit has one, explaining why McFadden's pseudo R
squared is `NA`. Other notes in this walkthrough record where the robust
covariance is used, the per-factor reporting of an additive model, Bonferroni
intervals beside Holm p-values, and differences rather than ratios under the
inverse link.

## Reporting the result

```{r report-values, include = FALSE}
tga <- fit$anova
ga <- gam$anova
tph <- fit$posthoc
row_of <- function(x) tph[tph$contrast == x, ]
r05 <- row_of("dose0.5 OJ - dose0.5 VC")
r1 <- row_of("dose1 OJ - dose1 VC")
r2 <- row_of("dose2 OJ - dose2 VC")
ms <- gph[gph$contrast == "Midsize / Small", ]
```

These write-ups are built from the fits with inline R, so the numbers cannot
drift from the analysis:

> A two-way analysis of variance (Type II) found that odontoblast length
> depended on the dose of vitamin C,
> F(`r tga$df[1]`, `r tga$df[4]`) = `r f2(tga$statistic[1])`,
> p `r fp(tga$p_value[1])`,
> partial η² = `r f2(fit$effect_sizes$partial_eta_sq[1])`, and on the
> supplement, F(`r tga$df[2]`, `r tga$df[4]`) =
> `r f2(tga$statistic[2])`, p `r fp(tga$p_value[2])`, with an interaction
> between them, F(`r tga$df[3]`, `r tga$df[4]`) = `r f2(tga$statistic[3])`,
> p `r fp(tga$p_value[3])`. Orange juice produced longer odontoblasts than
> ascorbic acid at 0.5 mg/day (difference `r f2(r05$estimate)`,
> Tukey-adjusted p `r fp(r05$p_adjusted)`) and 1 mg/day
> (`r f2(r1$estimate)`, adjusted p `r fp(r1$p_adjusted)`), but not at
> 2 mg/day (`r f2(r2$estimate)`, adjusted p `r fp(r2$p_adjusted)`).

> In a Gamma model with a log link, car prices differed by type,
> F(`r ga$df[1]`, `r ga$df[2]`) = `r f2(ga$statistic[1])`,
> p `r fp(ga$p_value[1])`, with type explaining
> `r round(100 * gam$effect_sizes$estimate[1])`% of the deviance. Midsize cars
> cost `r f2(ms$ratio)` times as much as small cars on average (`r 100 * gam$conf_level`% CI
> `r f2(ms$conf_low)` to `r f2(ms$conf_high)`, Tukey-adjusted).

For a model on a non-identity link, name the family and link, and report
comparisons in the form they take on it: ratios for a log link.
